biggestGap: The valley lines read SOFT AND SMOKY, not as crisp incised streams. The plain is no longer noise with scratches - it has broad interfluves and a connected drainage grain, and the mottle is subdued. But it is gentle organized ground with soft swales, not a convincing river plain. The cause is now KNOWN and is not a tuning problem: convergence thresholding on this flow guide cannot produce a dendritic network at fine scale - low thresholds give blobs, high thresholds give isolated spikes, and nothing between works. That needs a different network generator.
notes:
PLAIN - partial win, gate not met. Three plain cells rendered (3035, 1226, 3442), not one, so this is a method and not a tuned constant. The macro band is now a MONOTONE concave map of the flow guide, so the surface and the network are one field read twice and cannot disagree. Three real bugs fixed on the way: the accumulation proxy was pinned at its 0.30 floor over half of every window; the S term was missing from E=K*Q^m*S^n; a 0.70 threshold cut 40x steps that rendered as round holes.

MOUNTAIN - preserved, fault untouched. Reads as a dissected range with real crests and spurs. The flanks are still STREAKY and the snowy core has a crumpled-foil quality. Cause is known: the sub-cell structural-band term, which is also the one term whose author chose the geology first and built a field to express it.

COAST - preserved, not bit-identical (max |dH| 0.006). A first attempt SHATTERED it into an archipelago because that window entire island stands within 0.023 of the waterline, so the macro band WAS its land. The shore fade exists because of that failure.

TWO ROUTES FAILED and are recorded in the source so nobody repeats them: negating the peak field gives brain coral again (its crest web is squared, so broad, and a broad web upside down is lobes); stacking |n| as the mirror gives quilted leather (the zero set of a smooth field is closed loops).

NOT WIRED into generateRegion.ts by standing decision. 87 tests, seam 0 mismatches over 125,000 samples, 737-836 ms per window.
